title: Menelik's Victory at Adwa
text:
In 1889 Menelik II of Ethiopia signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy. The Amharic text said Ethiopia could use Italy for its foreign relations if it wished; the Italian text said it must. Italy used its version to claim a protectorate. Menelik rejected the claim, and in 1895 Italian forces from Eritrea advanced into northern Ethiopia.

Menelik had spent years preparing. He had imported large quantities of modern rifles and some artillery, and he had built alliances with regional rulers who had once been rivals. His wife, Empress Taytu, a firm opponent of any concession, commanded her own troops. When he called for mobilization, a very large army gathered and marched north, fighting the Italians at Amba Alage and besieging their fort at Mekele.

By late February 1896 the armies faced each other near Adwa. The Ethiopian force was several times larger, and both sides were short of supplies. Under pressure from Rome to win, the Italian commander, General Oreste Baratieri, decided to attack. On the night before 1 March his brigades advanced through the mountains with poor maps, lost touch with each other, and were destroyed one by one. Italy lost several thousand dead and many prisoners.

In the Treaty of Addis Ababa later that year, Italy recognized Ethiopia's full independence. Adwa became a symbol of resistance to colonialism across Africa.
lesson: Victory often goes to the side that prepared long before the battle: resources secured, allies united, and leaders agreed on what they will not concede.
people: Menelik II, Empress Taytu Betul, Oreste Baratieri
source: Raymond Jonas, The Battle of Adwa (2011); Harold Marcus, The Life and Times of Menelik II (1975)
